data.author: Known-Pace6739
data.body:
I validate before routing, and keep edge rejection as the last safety net. The producer should ideally emit a typed object already, using structured output/Pydantic rather than free text that the next node has to reverse-engineer.

Then I run deterministic semantic checks before committing it to shared state. If validation fails, I keep the raw output + validation error and send only that failure back for a bounded repair. The next node never sees half-valid state.

data.author: Future_AGI
data.body: The resume case settles more than any clean demo, and the fix that travels across both frameworks is an idempotency key on every side effect, run id plus node id, checked before the write. Stamping that same id as a trace tag on every state update also answers the which-agent-produced-this question without replaying anything. We treat the handoff record as the canonical state and trace every transition, the gateway and tracing layer that does it is open-source: [github.com/future-agi/future-agi](http://github.com/future-agi/future-agi)

data.author: Mariia_Sosnina
data.body: Right test. The bit that catches people is the idempotency key has to commit in the same transaction as the write, otherwise a retry that dies between the two still doubles it. Framework matters way lesss than that transaction boundary tbh.

data.author: Apart-Currency7380
data.body: If handoffs are the pain point, I'd go with LangGraph. CrewAI feels more natural for role based workflows, but LangGraph's explicit state, checkpoints, and retries make complex handoffs much easier to manage. Being able to control exactly what gets passed between agents is a huge advantage once context starts growing. My experience has been that as workflows get more complex, state management matters more than agent roles.

data.body: run\_id + node\_id solves duplicates writes, but the same ID could double as a trace tag, stamp it on every state update too, and you get also which agent, which attempt produced this value.

data.author: ParrotIntegrated
Mathie1729
data.body: Only as clean as what you actually put in graph state. If the agent stores its decision in a tool result or some scratch area outside the checkpoint, re-entering at step 3 can feel clean right up until the next agent asks what was decided and gets nothing. I'd treat graph state as the canonical handoff record, not just natural language transcript.

data.author: Michael_Jeffords
data.body: on that resume case LangGraph re-enters the node from the old checkpoint, so agent B writes twice unless you check the db or an idempotency key before the write. decisions and approvals that lived in graph state survive. the side effect does not get rolled back for you, which is what bit a \~12-node run when we marked done before the receipt landed

data.author: cmtape
data.body: CrewAI handoffs feel like handing off a Slack thread. Natural at first, then everyone scrolls the whole history to find the decision. LangGraph is like a lab notebook with a sign-out sheet — less magical, but you can re-enter at step 3 without replaying the whole show.

data.author: Smart_Ad500
data.body: I'd compare one failure case in both: agent B writes to the DB, then dies before reporting success. On resume, does it write twice? Which decisions and approvals survive? That would tell me more about the handoff than a clean demo where every agent finishes.

data.author: mostly_deterministic
data.body:
The LangGraph/LangChain ecosystem can give you the best of both worlds. Graphs when you have a deterministic topology in a workflow. LangChain direct agents when you want the LLM to drive execution more. 

I take a look at a few different types of workflows and who should own the control loop of each here: https://demianbrecht.com/posts/the-division-of-the-local-harnesses/

data.author: Known-Pace6739
data.body: For complicated systems I'd keep autonomy inside the nodes and make the edges deterministic. That pushes me toward LangGraph for the outer orchestration; CrewAI Flows can get close now with structured state and persistence.
